## Abstract

Image denoising is a fundamental problem in mobile photography. Despite a large number of solutions proposed for this task, the majority of them are trained on synthetically produced noisy images, and are additionally too computationally heavy for processing full-resolution images on mobile devices. This creates a need for efficient deep learning-based models that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can denoise Full HD resolution photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. More recently, deep learning-based approaches have demonstrated substantially improved quantitative performance [2, 3, 13, 23, 24, 60, 72, 73, 90, 91, 109, 111, 112]. However, despite achieving high fidelity metrics, many of these methods rely on synthetically generated training and validation datasets [13, 24, 72, 73, 90, 91, 109, 111, 112], or are evaluated on limited collections of indoor imagery [1–3, 60], thereby restricting their generalizability to real-world noisy camera data. Another primary limitation of these approaches is that they are typically focused on optimizing the restoration quality, while neglecting the computational efficiency required for mobile platforms, where resource constraints are a critical consideration. In this challenge, we directly address this problem and propose the participants to use a real-world dataset and design efficient image denoising models that can run on recent smartphone GPUs.

Designing deep learning models that run efficiently on mobile devices — especially across different AI accelerators like NPUs — is a complex challenge. It demands careful analysis of hardware constraints such as limited operator support, restricted memory capacity and bandwidth, reduced accuracy for quantized models and specific driver behavior of NPUs. Even when certain layers or operations are technically supported, they may be executed inefficiently due to constraints related to NPU hardware architecture or its driver implementation, and thus create performance bottlenecks during inference. A striking example here would be the Google Tensor NPU present in all recent Google Pixel smartphones that, despite having quite high theoretical peak performance, is unable to efficiently accelerate the vast majority of even simplistic CNN-based models [53]. As a result, achieving low latency and energy efficiency often requires partial or complete redesigns

# Three-Dimensional Stability of Weakly Asymmetric Burgers Vortices: A Circulation-Independent Asymmetry Threshold and Optimal Decay

J. Jia, T. Tao

> Abstract: Burgers vortices are stationary solutions of the Navier--Stokes equations in a background straining flow and serve as a model for vortex tubes in three-dimensional turbulence. In this paper, we consider weakly asymmetric strains and establish the local nonlinear asymptotic stability of the corresponding Burgers vortices against small three-dimensional perturbations for arbitrary circulation. Our proof exploits the specific axial structure of the linearized operator, combining a two-dimensional resolvent analysis with decay estimates for axial derivatives to control the full three-dimensional evolution. A first-moment decomposition isolates the slow modes, and Gaussian resolvent bounds are transferred to polynomially weighted spaces. This yields nonlinear stability with the endpoint exponential decay rate $(1-λ)/2$, where $λ$ denotes the strain asymmetry, without any additional polynomial factor in time. An exact nonlinear first-moment law demonstrates that this rate is optimal over the full admissible perturbation class, including at zero circulation.

### 2.3 Runtime Evaluation on the Target Platform

In this challenge, we use two flagship mobile SoCs as our target evaluation platforms: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and MediaTek Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno 840 and Arm Mali G1-Ultra MC12 GPUs, respectively, that can be found in numerous flagship smartphones. The models were parsed and accelerated using the TFLite GPU delegate [68] that demonstrated the best runtime results on both platforms. NPU runtimes provided for reference were obtained by running the models with the Qualcomm QNN and MediaTek Neuron TFLite delegates on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and the Dimensity 9500 SoCs. All final solutions were tested using the aforementioned AI Benchmark application.

### 2.4 Challenge Phases

The challenge consisted of the following phases:

  1. Development: the participants get access to the data and AI Benchmark app, and are able to train the models and evaluate their runtime locally;
## 3 Challenge Results

In this challenge, 7 teams entered the final phase and submitted their results, TFLite models, codes, executables and factsheets. Table 1 summarizes the final challenge results for both tracks and reports PSNR, SSIM and runtime numbers for the valid solutions on the final test dataset and on the target evaluation platform. The proposed methods are described in section 4, and the team members and affiliations are listed in Appendix A.

### 3.1 Results and Discussion

All submitted solutions demonstrated a very high efficiency: the majority of models are able to process Full HD (1920×1088 px) image under 150 milliseconds on both target GPUs. This shows great progress in both model design as well as in mobile AI acceleration hardware that is currently able to provide decent speed-up for many common network architectures. Team TLG is the challenge winner: solution proposed by this team was able to demonstrate over 35 and 19 FPS when running on the Adreno and Arm GPUs, respectively. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Challenge

The challenge combines a real-world noisy-clean image dataset with tools for local device testing and a common evaluation of denoising fidelity and runtime. Participants developed and submitted LiteRT models for evaluation on specified smartphone GPUs.

### 2. Challenge

  * The challenge asks participants to develop practical mobile AI solutions using real training data and tools for local runtime testing and debugging.The denoising task is framed around mobile-related deployment needs.Source: §2 · p. 2

### 2.1. Dataset

  * For each scene, 20 burst-mode photos were averaged into a clean reference, with more than 1,000 indoor and outdoor scenes captured under varied illumination.RAW 4000×3000 images were converted to RGB with noise correction disabled; about 650 scenes were used for training, with the remainder reserved for validation and testing.Source: §2.1 · pp. 2–3

### 2.2. Local Runtime Evaluation

  * AI Benchmark let participants load custom TensorFlow Lite models on Android devices and test available acceleration options locally.The supported options include delegates and CPU inference, enabling execution on smartphone NPUs, APUs, DSPs, GPUs, and CPUs.Source: §2.2 · p. 3, Figure 2 · p. 3

### 2.4. Challenge Phases

  * The challenge proceeded through development, validation, and final testing, with participants uploading models for validation and submitting final models, code, and factsheets.The phases also included local training and runtime evaluation, followed by validation leaderboard comparisons.Source: §2.4 · p. 4

### 2.5. Scoring System

  * Solutions were assessed using PSNR for fidelity, SSIM as a perceptual proxy, and runtime on both target GPUs.Organizers evaluated final submissions under identical conditions without giving participants access to the test dataset, addressing overfitting, reproducibility, and consistency concerns.Source: §2.5 · p. 4

## 3. Challenge Results

Seven teams submitted final-stage solutions evaluated on the final test dataset and target platforms. TLG won on speed, TeamPAK achieved the highest fidelity, and direct PyTorch-to-TFLite conversion simplified development.

### 3.1. Results and Discussion

  * Over 35 FPS on Adreno and 19 FPS on Arm GPUs made TLG the challenge winner; Team Fanis was slightly slower, while TeamPAK achieved the highest fidelity.The final results covered valid solutions across both tracks and target platforms.Source: §3.1 · p. 4, §3 · p. 4
  * Most solutions processed Full HD (1920×1088 px) images in under 150 ms on both target GPUs; TeamPAK ran in under 50 ms on Qualcomm and MediaTek NPUs despite worse GPU latency.Source: §3.1 · p. 4
  * PyTorch models could be converted directly to TFLite without TensorFlow/Keras reimplementation or ONNX, simplifying mobile-friendly architecture development.Source: §3.1 · pp. 4–5

## 4. Challenge Methods

The finalist teams proposed distinct denoising architectures combining multiscale feature processing, residual paths, and mobile-oriented design choices.

### 4.1. TLG

  * TLG’s three-scale U-Net uses strided encoding, residual blocks, transposed-convolution decoding, symmetric skips, and a global input residual; it trains with L2 loss for 5,000 epochs.Source: §4.1 · p. 5

### 4.2. Fanis

  * Fanis’s two-scale FastSHADE [19] uses frequency-split AFDB branches, gated skip upsampling, and reparameterized convolutions; training adds SIDD-Medium and MIDD data.Training uses two stages, with Charbonnier loss followed by a PSNR-based loss; STE rounding supports directly quantized integer predictions.Source: §4.2 · pp. 5–6

### 4.3. TeamPAK

  * TeamPAK’s lightweight U-Net uses bottlenecked Lite Denoising Blocks, nearest-neighbor decoder upsampling, and all-ReLU activations, with a teacher-guided distillation workflow [26].The distillation loss weights teacher-output MSE at 900, compared with ground-truth MSE at 100 and L1 loss at 50.Source: §4.3 · p. 6

### 4.4. Z6

  * Z6’s AGDNet, based on GFAB [86], uses a fixed 24-channel attention-guided module and fused reparameterized blocks with a global input residual; it was trained on MAI2021 alone.Source: §4.4 · p. 6

### 4.5. IVCL

  * IVCL’s CSPID [94] integrates SAFM [89] multiscale branches into eight residual CSP blocks and trains on Mobile AI 2021 data.The CSP blocks maintain 64 intermediate channels, while SAFM routes features through branches downsampled by factors of 2, 4, and 8.Source: §4.5 · pp. 6–7
